name: Tomato Leaf Mold
causal_agent: Passalora fulva (syn. Fulvia fulva, Cladosporium fulvum)
symptoms: leaves: Yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces Fuzzy olive-green to gray mold growth on lower leaf surfaces Leaves may curl and become distorted Severe infections can cause defoliation stems: Occasionally stems can be infected, but disease is mostly foliar
management: cultural: Use drip irrigation and avoid wetting foliage Space plants to improve air circulation Stake, string, or prune plants to reduce humidity around leaves Circulate air in greenhouses/high tunnels with vents, fans, or by rolling up sides Maintain night temperatures higher than outside to reduce dew formation Remove and destroy crop residue at the end of the season; sanitize greenhouse surfaces and equipment resistant_varieties: Use resistant cultivars cautiously, as resistance is often race-specific Test resistant varieties on a small scale before large-scale planting Reference: Cornell Disease Resistant Vegetable Varieties list chemical: Apply fungicides preventively when conditions favor disease Rotate chemical families to prevent resistance development For organic production, copper-based products (e.g., Champ) can provide partial control Follow all pesticide labels and legal restrictions for greenhouse/high tunnel use
sources: Midwest Vegetable Production Guide for Commercial Growers, 2023
Minnesota Extension, Tomato Leaf Mold Management
Jones, J.B., et al. 2014. Compendium of Tomato Diseases and Pests, 2nd Edition. APS Press.
